extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal researchers, librarians, attorneys, and members of the public researching federal administrative rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A concise, descriptive overview of federal rulemaking processes and sources, focusing on how agencies promulgate rules, the governing statutes (Administrative Procedure Act), and the notice-and-comment procedures. Intended to orient researchers to where rules are published and the basic legal constraints on agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules/Regulations — purpose and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative laws at the federal level are typically called rules (or regulations). Rules are promulgated to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy. The terms 'rules' and 'regulations' have the same meaning in the context of federal administrative law and are used interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that 'rules' are the agency-level instruments used to carry out statutes; when evaluating or producing rules, ensure they are framed as implementing, interpreting, or prescribing statutory law or policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official publication sources for rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules are published in two official sources: the Federal Register and the Code of Federal Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Federal Register to find proposed and final rule notices and supporting documents; use the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) to find the codified, current text of agency rules. Cite the appropriate source when referencing a rule's status (proposed vs. codified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency creation and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies are organizational arrangements created by Congress in order to carry out law and policy. Agencies provide the detailed rules and guidance needed in order to clarify and properly execute statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing rulemaking or drafting comments, recognize agencies as delegated implementers of Congressional statutes; evaluate whether the agency's actions align with the statute's purpose and the level of detail appropriate for agency expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation constraint — agencies must act within statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies cannot act unless Congress has delegated the authority for them to do so and must not act beyond that authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A core legal constraint on rulemaking is that agency rules must be traceable to a valid statutory delegation; challenge or evaluate rules for potential ultra vires action (acting beyond delegated authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking as the process for creating/amending/repealing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking is the process used by federal agencies in creating, amending, or repealing rules. Congress grants rulemaking authority to federal agencies in order to implement legislative statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rulemaking as the formal procedure by which agencies exercise delegated authority; understand stages (proposal, public input, finalization) when researching rule history or preparing submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal effect of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations issued pursuant to this authority carry the force and effect of law and can have substantial implications for policy implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that agency rules are not mere guidance but can be legally binding; when evaluating rules or advising clients/public, account for their mandatory legal effect and policy consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA governance and notice requirement (5 U.S.C. §553(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking is largely governed by standards set forth in the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 551 et seq.). Typically, an agency must give the public notice of a proposed rule before it goes into effect (5 U.S.C. § 553(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching or evaluating rulemaking, apply the APA's notice requirements — check that adequate notice was given in the Federal Register and that statutory procedures under §553 were followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice & comment (informal rulemaking) procedures (5 U.S.C. §553(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice is accomplished by publishing the proposed rule in the Federal Register. After the proposed rule is published, the public is given an opportunity to submit comments on the proposed rule (5 U.S.C. § 553(c)). The agency may take the comments into consideration before the final rule is published and takes effect. The entire process is frequently referred to as notice & comment rulemaking or informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For participation or evaluation, ensure the proposed rule was published in the Federal Register, identify the comment period and any supporting materials, and verify that the agency considered comments in its final rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal rulemaking (on-the-record hearings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking occurs when rules are required by statute to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing; this process happens much less frequently than informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish formal from informal rulemaking: where statute mandates formal procedures, expect an on-the-record hearing and a different evidentiary/record standard; verify statutory triggers for formal rulemaking when assessing procedural adequacy.
